newsitem.title: USA: Kirlin Securities pulls Sprint Spectrum bond ad.
newsitem.headline: Kirlin Securities pulls Sprint Spectrum bond ad.

text.p: Kirlin Securities Inc. said Monday it has agreed to pull ads for junk bonds issued by an affiliate of Sprint Corp. after the affiliate complained the New York-area broker's ads might confuse consumers.

"Kirlin Securities has pulled the Sprint advertisement in its entirety," said Patrice Vellecca, director of compliance at Kirlin, which is based in Syosset, N.Y., on Long Island. She said Kirlin was looking into the matter internally and would take appropriate action, but declined to elaborate.

Last week, Sprint Spectrum L.P., an affiliate of Sprint Corp., asked Kirlin to stop broadcasting the ads, which included references to the long-distance telephone company's familiar "pin-drop" ad campaign and its spokewoman, Candice Bergen.

Junk bonds from Sprint Spectrum, which provides digital personal communications services, are rated "highly speculative" by major credit rating agencies. By comparison, Sprint Corp. bonds are considered "investment grade" by bond rating agencies.
While Sprint Spectrum is 40 percent owned by Sprint, the long-distance telephone company is not associated with Sprint Spectrum debt and has no obligation regarding its payment.
Kirlin, based in Syosset, N.Y., had been running the ad on local radio stations since June and had planned to continue the campaign for the next two weeks, a Kirlin official said.
A spokesman for Sprint Spectrum said the ads were misleading and misrepresented the issuer of the bonds.

"Obviously, they are using some of the messages from Sprint Corp., mixed in with some of the key messages from Sprint Spectrum. We want to be sure that no one is misled," a Sprint Spectrum spokesman said last week.
Sprint Spectrum first became aware of the ad campaign when it was brought to the company's attention by a reporter for Reuters.
The firm has been the subject of various disciplinary actions in the past several years, according to the National Association of Securities Dealers.
Since 1991, Kirlin has settled via arbitration three cases involving misrepresentation of securities and omission of facts, according to the association, a self-regulatory body for brokers.
